Which paragraph contains the following information?

NB You may use any letter more than once.

Questions 6-9

Complete the summary below.

Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
groups.content:
Benefits of sponge cities

Sponge cities can reduce the risk of flooding, refill the [6] beneath the city and make streets cooler in summer. They also create new habitats for wildlife.

There are social benefits as well. New green spaces give people more opportunities for physical [7], and doctors in some countries encourage patients suffering from stress or [8] to spend time in green areas. Cooler neighbourhoods can also reduce heat-related illness among [9] residents.

Questions 31-36

Complete the summary using the list of phrases, A-J, below.

Write the correct letter, A-J, in boxes 31-36 on your answer sheet.

A   modest fame
B   vast wealth
C   remarkable discovery
D   research methods
E   select group
F   professional opportunities
G   public debate
H   hazardous work
I   biographer's perspective
J   narrow interest
groups.content:
Mary Anning's life and work

From a [31], one of the most interesting things about Anning is that, although she made major discoveries, she had very little formal education. Her [32] were limited because, as a woman, she could not join scientific societies or attend university. However, when she found the first complete plesiosaur in 1823, she already enjoyed [33] among geologists. About twelve years earlier, she had made a [34] with her brother, and she carried out [35] on the cliffs near her home. Her fossils had also attracted the attention of a [36] of wealthy geologists.

questions.explanation: Answer: D Paragraph D: ' several obstacles must be overcome ': maintenance, new skills, cooperation between departments, land ownership and disruption.
Answer: C Paragraph C: ' The Dutch city of Rotterdam has been experimenting with such ideas since the early 2000s. '
Answer: E Paragraph E: ' the most successful projects need to be studied carefully and repeated elsewhere '.
Answer: B Paragraph B: ' Sponge city features work best when they are combined with other green measures. ' Green roofs, street trees and rain gardens create a network.
Answer: D Paragraph D: ' those who pay for the projects must be convinced that they represent good value . Economic arguments therefore remain essential'.
Answer: groundwater Paragraph A: benefits include 'the refilling of groundwater beneath the city'.

Answer: exercise Paragraph B: 'New parks and wetlands give people more places to walk, cycle and exercise '. The gap needs a general word; 'walk' and 'cycle' are only two examples, and only 'exercise' covers them all.
Answer: anxiety Paragraph B: doctors 'encourage patients with stress or anxiety to spend time in green spaces'.
Answer: elderly Paragraph B: cooler neighbourhoods 'reduce heat-related illness among elderly residents'.

text.en: a lower cost of construction
less need for regular maintenance
more room to store water
space for a wider range of plants
fewer disagreements about land ownership

questions.explanation: Answer: C, D In new districts, planners ' can leave room for large underground tanks that hold rainwater ' (C) and set aside land for planting, ' allowing a far greater variety of trees and shrubs ' (D). Cost, maintenance and land ownership are not mentioned in C.

text.en: to provide homes for wildlife
to grow food for local people
to reduce noise from traffic
to produce energy
to supply drinking water to other areas

questions.explanation: Answer: A, D Constructed wetlands filter pollution ' while providing homes for birds, insects and amphibians ' (A), and floating solar panels ' generate electricity ' (D).

text.en: who first developed the idea of learning styles
when views about how people learn began to change
why intelligence tests became less popular
how scientists measured intelligence in the early twentieth century

questions.explanation: Answer: B ' From the 1980s onwards, however, this view began to give way to a very different idea ': that people differ in how they learn best.

text.en: set personal targets for their learning.
work with classmates who have different strengths.
think of themselves as a particular kind of learner.
try a variety of study methods.

questions.explanation: Answer: C ' some teachers encourage students to describe themselves as 'visual learners' or 'hands-on learners' ' and choose study methods accordingly.

text.en: become more competitive with their classmates.
lose confidence in their teachers.
need more encouragement to work hard.
avoid tasks that they believe do not suit them.

questions.explanation: Answer: D Students labelled as kinaesthetic learners ' began to avoid tasks involving reading, believing that such tasks simply did not suit them '.
Answer: C (Paul Grady) Grady: the studies ' relied almost entirely on students' own reports of how they liked to learn , which tell us very little'.
Answer: B (Ruth Callan) ' She argues that her work has been widely misunderstood. '
Answer: A (Harold Finch) Finch ' argued in the 1920s that a child's intellectual ability was set at birth '.
Answer: E (Reyes and Lindqvist) They argue that presenting information in several ways ' should be done without drawing students' attention to their supposed style '.
Answer: B (Ruth Callan) 'It was meant to help students think about how they study. It was never supposed to be a way of making lessons more entertaining. '
Answer: D (Linda Moss) Moss: matching teaching to styles ' made no measurable difference to test results in any of our trials '.
Answer: YES Callan ' has responded to these criticisms thoughtfully, and she deserves credit for acknowledging the weaknesses in the evidence'.
Answer: NO The writer says the opposite: ' success has a much greater effect on students' confidence than their beliefs about themselves have on their success '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The writer discusses the research evidence but says nothing about how the media have reported the debate.
Answer: YES ' Attempts to match teaching to these preferences may even do more harm than good '.
Answer: NOT GIVEN The writer says Anning's finds helped to establish that groups of animals had disappeared, but does not say what most geologists believed before.
Answer: YES Paragraph 1: her discoveries ' were the subject of heated debate among scientists during her lifetime '.
Answer: NO Paragraph 2: ' She did not simply dig up fossils; she studied the anatomy of living animals ... in order to understand the creatures she found.'
Answer: NO Paragraph 2: modern palaeontology ' is built on the careful observation and collection of evidence that Anning practised '.

Answer: I (biographer's perspective) The writer, a biographer, says: ' When I began to research Anning's life, one of the things that intrigued me most was that... she received almost no formal education'.
Answer: F (professional opportunities) ' the scientific societies of the time were closed to her, and she could not attend university or publish her findings under her own name'.
Answer: A (modest fame) By 1823 ' she was already known to a number of geologists ': some fame, but limited.
Answer: C (remarkable discovery) 'Some twelve years earlier, she and her brother had found the first skeleton of an ichthyosaur to be recognised by scientists'.
Answer: H (hazardous work) She worked on the cliffs ' where landslides were a constant danger and once almost killed her '.
Answer: E (select group) 'she had also come to the attention of a small circle of wealthy gentlemen geologists '.

text.en: explaining why she decided to write the book
recommending that readers read the whole book
suggesting why Anning changed her interests so often
describing which of Anning's discoveries interested her most

questions.explanation: Answer: B The chapters 'make much more sense together than on their own, and I would encourage readers to follow her life from beginning to end '.

text.en: She spent most of her life in the same place.
She kept detailed records of her discoveries.
She often travelled to meet other scientists.
She published several articles about her work.

questions.explanation: Answer: A ' She rarely left Lyme Regis, making only one known visit to London '. Few letters survive (B) and she published only one short piece (D).

text.en: Their discoveries were more important than Anning's.
They were more confident about their ideas than Anning.
Their work caused more controversy than Anning's.
It is easier to write about their lives than about Anning's.

questions.explanation: Answer: D Darwin left thousands of documents, and ' The more such material a person leaves, the easier it is for a biographer '; for Anning, the biographer must 'read between the lines'.

text.en: People should plan their lives more carefully.
Good intentions are not enough to succeed.
Circumstances shape people's lives more than their own choices.
People should take advantage of every opportunity.

questions.explanation: Answer: C People have 'far less control over the direction of their lives than they imagine'; ' much of what happens to us is shaped by circumstances '.
